claims.text: The baseline FeNiCrCoCu coating contains pronounced Cu-rich segregated regions.
Cu-rich segregated regions can produce localized soft regions in the baseline coating.
Changing the cooling rate during deposition will reduce Cu-rich phase segregation relative to the baseline.
Reduced Cu-rich segregation will produce a more homogeneous elemental distribution.
A more uniform microstructure minimizes weak, soft phases that serve as preferential sites for localized plastic deformation.
Reducing Cu-rich segregated zones increases the coating's effective hardness.
Increasing effective hardness reinforces resistance to wear-induced plasticity during sliding.
At approximately 650°C, the modified coating will exhibit less microscopic deformation than the baseline coating under otherwise identical sliding conditions.
At approximately 650°C, the modified coating will exhibit a lower wear rate than the baseline coating under otherwise identical sliding conditions.
The standard deposition process produces noticeable Cu-rich segregated regions.
Cu-rich segregation in the baseline is associated with decreased high-temperature wear performance.
The predicted effects are expected to hold near 650°C under an inert or mildly oxidizing controlled atmosphere.
Changes in atmospheric composition may alter microstructural stability or wear mechanisms.
Significant changes in applied stress may alter microstructural stability or wear mechanisms.
Changing the cooling rate may also alter residual stresses and secondary microstructural features.
The comparison will use baseline and modified-cooling-rate coatings tested under the same approximately 650°C sliding conditions.
The hypothesis is falsified if confirmed reduction in Cu segregation is not accompanied by a statistically significant reduction in microscopic deformation or wear rate.
